title: Windows Autorun-around
subtitle: Why disabling Windows Autorun never really worked, and how to actually turn it off
description: For years, disabling Windows Autorun didn't fully work, and the Conficker worm's USB spread finally forced Microsoft to fix it in February 2009. Steve dissects the bit-encoded NoDriveTypeAutorun registry value, shows that setting it to FF disables every drive type, and reveals the key omission in Microsoft's own documentation: a value under CURRENT_USER silently overrides the one under LOCAL_MACHINE. Plus a still-unpatched Excel zero-day, a WMF metafile fix, the Adobe Reader patch, data-file exploits, .gov going DNSSEC, the Tigger trojan, and Conficker's jump to 50,000 domains.

chapters.title: Vote for Your Favorite Security Podcast

beats.t: A favor to ask listeners: there's an awards announcement at this year's RSA conference, and voting is at SocialSecurityAwards.com, named for social media, not the government program. Annoyingly for us, you must enable JavaScript, and a second "vote monkey" script, to vote.
Not very security-aware of them. They probably use cookies, and maybe Flash cookies, to stop repeat voting.

Cookies are part of HTTP itself, older than JavaScript. I voted once; it logged me and wouldn't even let me back to read the other entries. I won't tell people how to vote, just vote for your favorite security podcast.
And I'll happily accept when we win. Brian Krebs's "Security Fix" blog gets my vote too.

chapters.title: Patch Tuesday: Still No Excel Fix

beats.t: March's Patch Tuesday came and went, and the bad Excel zero-day we covered is still unpatched while being actively exploited. The security community wants Microsoft to ship an out-of-cycle fix rather than wait until April, because proof-of-concept code is circulating and opening a malicious spreadsheet runs code.

What we did get includes a critical fix for a parsing bug in the Windows Metafile formats, WMF and EMF, during the user-mode-to-kernel handoff in GDI, so a malicious metafile can run code. It requires a reboot, so do it.

beats.title: The Windows Metafile returns
beats.t: WMF/EMF are old vector image formats whose parser has produced several serious Windows flaws over the years, because image files are processed deep in the graphics stack. Like the data-file exploits elsewhere in this episode, it shows that "just an image" is not automatically safe.

chapters.title: Adobe Reader Patched, and Foxit's JBIG2

beats.t: The Adobe Acrobat flaw's patch shipped on the 11th, for version 9 only; versions 7 and 8 follow about a week later. It's a zero-day already exploited in the wild. Note that disabling Reader's JavaScript no longer protects you, non-JavaScript exploits for the bug now exist.

Foxit was asked if it shares the flaw. It said the bug was a buffer overflow in Adobe's JBIG2 decoder; Foxit uses its own decoder and isn't vulnerable the same way, you'd get an empty image instead of a crash. But Foxit still shipped an update after taking a closer look.

It's Mozilla update time too: Firefox 3.0.7, past-vulnerable Thunderbird and SeaMonkey, plus Opera after 9.63. And Winamp: its open-source Libsndfile sample parser has an integer-overflow bug, so update past Winamp 5.55.
It's scary when the exploit is in a data file. Everyone knows to avoid executables and to back up data, so a JPG, PDF or MP3 feels harmless.

Someone wrote that MP3-sample parser to make sound come out, not with security in mind. A specially crafted file overflows an integer, jumps execution into the rest of the buffer, and that buffer is the attacker's program. The grim reality is this is now big business: machines are taken over for profit, not curiosity.

beats.title: Why "just a data file" isn't safe
beats.t: Any program that parses a complex file, images, PDFs, audio, spreadsheets, can be tricked by a malformed one into overrunning a buffer and executing attacker-supplied bytes. Backing up only your data protects your files, but a booby-trapped data file can still compromise the machine that opens it.

chapters.title: .gov Goes DNSSEC, and a Lingering Kaminsky Flaw

beats.t: As of the end of February, all the government's top-level .gov DNS servers run DNSSEC, which they never had before. It's complex to set up, so almost nobody bothers, but now anyone wanting verifiable, non-spoofable signed records from .gov can get them. It doesn't help .com or .net, but it's a step.
One of this month's Microsoft patches also fixed a lingering Kaminsky-style cache-poisoning flaw in Microsoft's DNS server.

beats.title: DNSSEC adoption
beats.t: DNSSEC cryptographically signs DNS records so resolvers can detect forged answers, the cache-poisoning class Dan Kaminsky publicized in 2008. Adoption was slow for years; the DNS root itself was not signed until mid-2010, well after .gov here.

chapters.title: The Tigger Trojan Targets Stock Traders

beats.t: Brian Krebs wrote up the "Tigger" trojan, notable for being tightly targeted: over a quarter-million Windows machines infected, and it specifically goes after employees and clients of E*TRADE, ING Direct, Vanguard, optionsXpress, TD Ameritrade and Scottrade.

It uses a privilege-escalation exploit Microsoft patched back in October 2008, yet it still spreads five months later. Because it elevates privilege, even running under a limited user account doesn't protect an unpatched machine.

The Downadup/Conficker/Kido worm, found in a Symantec honeypot in November 2008, has infected at least 11.4 million PCs by a neutral SRI International census, and about three million are actively phoning home each day. It builds a botnet that updates itself by contacting generated domain names.

Defenders fight it by pre-registering or blocking those domains. The original version generated 250 candidate domains a day, which was blockable. The new C variant jumps that to 50,000, so defenders must cover 50,000 names a day; miss one and the worm updates.

The B variant is what forced Microsoft's hand: it spreads over network shares, by guessing 240 common passwords, and by writing an autorun.inf to USB sticks. Insert an infected stick into a machine whose Autorun wasn't truly disabled, and it runs, which is exactly the bug we're covering today.
So that's convenient, we're talking about Autorun today.

A listener shared his "hard drive paranoia" setup: SpinRite run quarterly on his internal and backup drives, a full offsite backup every weekend, Carbonite on the system drive, and every Drobo disk SpinRite-tested before install. Every time, he wakes to "No problems detected."

Notice his friends have the failures, because they do no preventative maintenance; he runs SpinRite preemptively. Letting it have a drive overnight each quarter lets it find and retire sectors that are becoming marginal before they turn unreadable.
That really was your original intent, a maintenance tool.
It is, though people won't buy it that way; they buy it when they need it, then run it quarterly forever after.

Now the main event. Disabling Windows Autorun is one of the first things a security-aware person does, and for years it was simply broken: you could configure it correctly and code would still run from CDs, USB sticks, network shares and more. US-CERT confirmed that the Autorun and NoDriveTypeAutorun values did not fully disable it.

Microsoft knew, but only offered a manual fix for Vista and Server 2008, which almost nobody installed. They feared that pushing a fix would "break" behaviors people had come to rely on, even though it was the behavior users had asked to disable.

Then Conficker started spreading through Autorun, infecting even people who had turned it off, so in February Microsoft finally pushed the fix to everyone, adding a HonorAutorunSetting key (default 1) so you can fall back to the old broken behavior if the fix breaks something.

The control is the registry value NoDriveTypeAutorun, and each drive type is a bit in a one-byte value. Bit 0x01 disables unknown-type drives (and oddly 0x80 does the same). Bit 0x04 disables removable drives, which covers USB and Firewire. Bit 0x08 disables fixed hard drives.

Bit 0x10 disables network-share drives, the one that was broken before. Bit 0x20 disables CD-ROM/DVD, and 0x40 disables RAM disks. The old 0x02 "no root directory" bit was deprecated and left unassigned.

Set every bit, hex FF (255), and Microsoft says all drive types are disabled. If you want to allow one type, say CD-ROMs, you leave its bit clear. Most people just want everything off, so FF is the answer.

Here's the critical omission. Microsoft documents only NoDriveTypeAutorun under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...\Policies\Explorer. But the same value can exist under HKEY_CURRENT_USER, and when it does, it completely overrides the LOCAL_MACHINE value, the bits aren't OR'd or AND'd, the user key simply wins.

So you can set LOCAL_MACHINE to FF, think you're protected, and not be, because a permissive CURRENT_USER value (often left by Tweak UI or similar tools) takes precedence. Microsoft's page, KB 967715, never mentions this.

My advice: set NoDriveTypeAutorun to FF under CURRENT_USER, or under both. A tiny .reg file can create and set the key. Set only LOCAL_MACHINE and a stray permissive CURRENT_USER value will silently defeat you.
You'd think the machine-wide setting would win, but per-user settings override, so CURRENT_USER takes precedence, then LOCAL_MACHINE.

beats.title: Default values differed
beats.t: Windows 2000 and Server 2003 defaulted NoDriveTypeAutorun to 0x95, which disabled removable (and network and unknown) drives. XP, Vista and Server 2008 defaulted to 0x91, deliberately re-enabling removable-drive Autorun, which is exactly the behavior Conficker exploited via USB sticks.

quiz.q: Why did Microsoft finally push the Autorun fix to all Windows versions in February 2009?
options: The Conficker worm was spreading via Autorun and infecting even people who had tried to disable it
A court ordered Microsoft to fix it
Windows 7 required the change
Antivirus vendors could no longer detect the worm
quiz.explain: Disabling Autorun had never fully worked; Conficker's USB and network-share spread exploited that, so Microsoft stopped leaving the fix as a manual, Vista-only download.

quiz.q: To disable Autorun on every drive type, what should NoDriveTypeAutorun be set to?
options: Hex FF (all bits set)
Hex 00 (all bits clear)
Hex 01
Hex 91
quiz.explain: Each bit disables one drive type; setting all eight bits (FF, 255) disables Autorun for unknown, removable, fixed, network, CD-ROM and RAM-disk drives.

quiz.q: What critical detail did Microsoft's documentation omit about disabling Autorun?
options: A NoDriveTypeAutorun value under HKEY_CURRENT_USER overrides the one under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
You must reboot twice for it to take effect
The value must be decimal, not hex
Only administrators can read the key
quiz.explain: Microsoft documented only the LOCAL_MACHINE key, but a value under CURRENT_USER silently takes precedence, so a stray permissive user value defeats a correct machine-wide setting.

quiz.q: Why does disabling JavaScript no longer protect Adobe Reader against the current flaw?
options: Non-JavaScript exploits for the same underlying bug now exist
Adobe removed the JavaScript setting
The flaw is in the JavaScript engine itself and can't be disabled
JavaScript was never the attack vector
quiz.explain: Disabling JavaScript blocked only the original exploitation path; the underlying JBIG2 decoder bug can now be triggered without JavaScript.

quiz.q: How did Conficker's C variant make it much harder for defenders to block?
options: It raised the number of generated command-and-control domains from 250 to 50,000 per day
It encrypted the entire hard drive
It stopped using domains and used email instead
It disabled Windows Update permanently
quiz.explain: Defenders must pre-register or block the worm's daily domains; jumping from 250 to 50,000 names a day makes covering them all impractical, and missing one lets the botnet update.

quiz.q: Why can't backing up only your data files guarantee you're safe from today's threats?
options: A malformed data file (image, PDF, audio) can exploit the parser that opens it and run code
Data files are too large to back up reliably
Backups always include hidden executables
Antivirus can't scan data files
quiz.explain: Parsers for complex formats can be tricked into buffer overflows, so opening a booby-trapped MP3, PDF or spreadsheet can compromise the machine even though it's "just data."
